column2: Chen had not been in bed long when a young apprentice knocked and brought him a letter just delivered by the night passenger boat. It was from Hu Xueyan. In a few brief lines, Hu said that he had heard of Yu Si's bereavement and was deeply concerned. He had made time for a special journey to Huzhou to offer his condolences and would take a boat the very day he sent the letter. All Chen's worries vanished. With Hu coming, nothing need trouble him any longer. He slept soundly, then slipped down to the wharf early the next morning to wait. It was after ten when Hu arrived. Once the boat had anchored and the gangplank was in place, Chen went aboard. “Mr Hu!” he called with a smile. “I never expected you to come. This is wonderful.” His manner told Hu that he had arrived at just the right moment: something needed his attention. He nodded. “I've hired a boat for the journey, and I have only three days. Come, sit down. Let's go through everything first.”

The conversation proved a long one. From Yu's loss of his son, Chen passed to his household troubles; from A’qi to his own difficulties; and from himself to Huang Yi. Naturally, he also told Hu how Yu had put aside all past grievances and undertaken to arrange Chen's wedding, how Yu had formally met the bride's family and delivered the betrothal money, and how A’zhu's mother wished to prepare her daughter's dowry, which meant postponing the wedding until the following year. He concluded, “I must ask you to decide everything for me.” “Who would have thought so many complications could arise the moment I left?” Hu frowned deeply and considered for some time before speaking. “Your wedding can be arranged one way or another. We can discuss that later. Your Fourth Uncle Yu's situation is more troublesome. I've never met his daughter. What do you think of her? Is she naturally kind?” “Sister A’lan has long been known for her intelligence and ability. As for her nature...” Chen chose his words carefully. “Surely she can't be too unkind. She's his only daughter.” “And now his only surviving child. I don't think she would fail in her duty to him—or dare to.” The last words were not immediately clear. On reflection, Chen understood their weight. If A’lan dared to mistreat her elderly father, Hu would certainly intervene as her father's friend. At the very least, he would advise Yu not to give her a single copper. “A married daughter is water poured away”: however fiercely she fought at her parents' home, that would not secure her the property.

“Mr Hu,” Chen said, struck by an idea, “why not help Fourth Uncle put his household affairs in order?” Hu considered in silence. Clearly, the proposal deserved thought. Given his own temperament and his friendship with Yu, he could hardly stand aside. Yet once he intervened, he must see the whole affair properly settled. Three days would not be enough; even another day or two might not suffice. Meanwhile, business in Shanghai and Hangzhou would suffer. Like a hunchback taking a tumble, with both ends left in the air, he would fail on both fronts. That would be foolish indeed. “And there's A’qi,” Chen added with a troubled face. “She's a nuisance. I wasn't afraid of her before; she could do as she pleased. But now I can't go rolling in the mud with her. What am I to do?” Such was the predicament of men who had made their way on the streets. Who did not wish to better himself? Once a man had acquired a little standing, he wanted to rise and become respectable. Yet emerging from the mud without a stain was difficult. Old connections tugged at him. He might value his good name and refuse to roll in the mire, but others clung to him and would not let go; in the end he remained involved in the same disreputable ways. Hu understood this thoroughly and would naturally find a way to help Chen. Yu's household was one difficult problem, Chen's predicament another. Together, the two suddenly gave Hu an idea. He stood up. “Come. Let's go ashore.”

Seeing the pleased look of discovery on Hu's face, Chen knew that another ingenious plan was forming. “Mr Hu,” he asked with a smile, “you must have thought of something nobody else would imagine. Could you tell me first?” “There's no reason not to. I mean to have A’qi moor her boat at the old landing.” Chen was startled. Then, thinking it through, he felt profound admiration. He had long known that Yu could not do without A’qi. Their enforced separation was entirely the work of A’lan and her husband. If the broken mirror could be made whole again, then, quite apart from A’qi's feelings, Yu would at least cease to be so dejected. Naturally, Chen's own troubles would vanish too. “Mr Hu, sometimes we fail to see things clearly and can't understand why. Now I know. There's only a sheet of paper between us and the answer, thin enough to pierce with a finger, yet we simply can't see it!” “Don't flatter me. We don't know yet whether it will work. Let me first find out how matters stand. We'll go and see your Fourth Uncle.”

Chen went ashore and hired two sedan chairs at the wharf to carry them straight to Yu's house. Getting out first, he hurried inside and found Yu drinking alone in low spirits. He greeted him, then announced, “Mr Hu is here!” Delight and surprise instantly appeared on Yu's face. “Where?” he asked, rising. “He's come straight here from the boat. He made the journey especially to see you, Fourth Uncle.” As Chen spoke, Hu had already entered the inner gate. Yu hurried to meet him. They clasped hands and looked at one another, each seemingly with a thousand things to say and no idea where to begin. At last Hu said, “Brother Yu, don't grieve so.” Until then Yu had held himself together. Those words touched the heart of his sorrow, and tears streamed down his face. Stamping his foot, he cried, “There's no point in living!” Between broken sobs, he went on: without a true friend, he could not even have a proper cry. He had so much on his mind and nobody to tell; all his suffering could not be expressed at once. Now that Hu had come, he would explain everything to him, resign his post at the yamen, and find somewhere quiet to eat vegetarian food and recite the Buddha's name for the rest of his days. “Brother Yu, Brother Yu! There's no need for that!” Hu kept repeating. With these consoling words, he half supported and half led Yu indoors. A’lan came out to greet him. Although they had never met, she had long heard his name and knew that he was an influential friend of her father's. She was therefore scrupulously courteous, attending to him for a while before having fresh dishes and wine prepared and asking him to stay for a simple meal.

At the table, Hu listened to Yu's complaints and said little. He wanted to hear more, and this was not the place for a confidential discussion. Only after Yu had poured out his distress and begun to look somewhat revived did Hu say, “Brother Yu, there are a few things I'd like to say in confidence.” “Ah!” Yu understood. “Let's go and sit at my bank.” At Jucheng Bank, with nobody else in Yu's private room, they reclined together on the opium couch and spoke quietly. Hu's first question was, “Brother Yu, what exactly happened with A’qi?” Yu gave a long sigh, then paused for some time. “I don't know where to begin. This affair...” He shook his head and sighed again. From his expression and manner, Hu could complete the unfinished sentence: I was wrong. Clearly, his question had touched the sore spot. There was no need for further indirect probing. “Brother Yu,” he said plainly, “I'll get A’qi back for you.” Yu raised his head and stared, as though he could not understand and thought Hu must be joking. But of course he was not. Hu never joked about such things. Even if it were a joke, Yu believed he had the means to make it real. He needed only to consider his own position.

“There would be a great many difficulties...” “No!” Hu interrupted. “You needn't concern yourself with those. I know the difficulties you mean. First, you're afraid A’lan and A’qi won't get on. Second, you're afraid A’qi is still angry and will deliberately make herself difficult to please. Neither is a problem. Leave them to me, and I'll arrange everything properly. It depends only on you. If you're determined to act out Water Spilled Before the Horse and refuse to take her back, there's nothing more to discuss. Otherwise, leave it all to me. Tell me what you think.” “With a friend like you, what more can I say?” “That's settled, then. Your word is all I need. Lie here and rest. I'll have a word with Shilong and come straight back.” Hu rose from the couch, found Chen, and drew him aside to give him detailed instructions in private. Only after Chen had left to carry them out did Hu return.

“Brother Yu, let me say this first. If I speak too bluntly about your family affairs, will you be offended?” “What a thing to ask! With our friendship, even if you reproached me outright, I should listen.” “Then I'll speak frankly. Everyone says that daughter of yours is extremely formidable. Is it true?” “Yes.” Yu nodded. “I'm on my guard against her myself.” “It's a miserable thing to have to guard against your own flesh and blood all the time. Let's speak openly. Men die for wealth as birds die for food. Whatever the twists and turns, it's all about money. I advise you to take this opportunity to divide the estate. Give your daughter a share too, so that she needn't keep scheming. Wouldn't that settle things neatly?” “Yes, yes.” Yu nodded slowly. “That is one way. Go on. You must have more to say.” “There are different ways to divide an estate. First I must ask whether you've made any plans yourself.”

“What plans could I have? When A’hu died, my heart turned to ice. I wished I could become a monk. Whatever they said was good enough for me. I'd abandoned everything; they could do as they pleased. But...” Yu paused, visibly moved. “When Little Monk came and I heard how he was getting on, I began to feel a little happier. And today you've made time to travel all this way to see me. It makes me think there are still some good things in this world. To tell you the truth, only now am I beginning to find a little pleasure in being alive.” These were words from the heart. Hu felt comforted and all the more determined to do his utmost. “Brother Yu, since you think so well of me, I can't avoid taking a hand. I might as well go further. We must plan for the whole household. However many difficulties there are, we mustn't shrink from them. Straighten your back, grit your teeth, and let's untangle everything at once. Shall we?” “Yes!” Yu answered eagerly. He too had tried to plan for his household, but the more he thought, the worse his head ached. He had never found the courage to sort out that tangled skein. Hu's words alone lifted a burden from him, and he already felt much better. “Then let's take things one at a time. First, what do you intend to do about your post at the yamen?”

The revenue clerk's post was hereditary. In his hands was a fish-scale register, recording every landowner in the county, the location and acreage of each holding, and the tax assessed on it. This provided an inexhaustible livelihood from generation to generation. Had A’hu lived, he would naturally have succeeded his father. Now Yu had no son. Even if he later had another, it would take twenty or thirty years to bring the child to manhood. Such a distant and uncertain prospect could not form the basis of a practical plan. That was why Yu had once considered resigning, an exceedingly rare step. Ordinarily, a natural son inherited the post; failing that, the clerk adopted a son. He might even transfer it for a high price, with the successor changing his surname before taking over. Yu no longer meant to resign, but what should he do instead? He could not decide. With Hu there, he could not be bothered to rack his brains. He simply shook his head. “I don't know.” “Very well. My second question concerns your daughter-in-law. What arrangements do you intend to make for her?”

“That is my greatest difficulty!” Yu put down his opium pipe and sat up abruptly. “Think of it: she's only nineteen, and she has no son. How can she remain a widow?” “What does she want herself?” “Naturally, she wants to remain faithful to her husband.” “The longer a widow keeps that vow, the harder it becomes. Plenty have held out until their forties and then faltered. Brother Yu, let me speak frankly. We aren't some great scholarly family. We can afford to take a broader view. Besides, earning a chastity arch for a son to be proud of has some point. With no son and nothing to look forward to, leave aside whether she could keep the vow: even if she won her arch, what pleasure would it give her?” “You put it clearly. I've made up my mind. We'd better persuade her to remarry. If there's a suitable man, I'll marry her off as my own daughter and give her a good dowry. But...” Yu frowned again. “What if she insists on remaining a widow?” Naturally, they could only respect her wishes and choose a nephew from the clan for her to adopt as a son. Yet what would happen afterwards? While Yu lived, there would be no difficulty. If he died in three or five years, however, the widow and her fatherless child might well be bullied.

Hu had already considered these difficulties for him. “With your standing outside the family, Brother Yu, there will be no shortage of people to look after your household when you're gone. But even an upright magistrate finds family disputes hard to judge. If your own clansmen cause trouble, outsiders can scarcely intervene.” Having identified the heart of the problem, he explained his plan. If A’hu's widow wished to remain unmarried, there must be someone to look after her after Yu's death: the future head of the household. Yu should find a young, capable man who was, above all, honest and kind, adopt him as a son, and have him take the surname Yu. He need not carry on Yu's ancestral line; his role would be to inherit the hereditary post. In return for this favour, he must undertake to care for A’hu's widow and her adopted son, as well as any young children A’qi might bear Yu. The plan covered everything, and Yu agreed entirely. The difficulty lay in finding someone to whom orphans could be entrusted. He had able assistants in the revenue office, but some were too old, already with families of their own, and could hardly become another man's adopted son. Others had ability but lacked character. While Yu lived, they would not dare misbehave; once he died, they would surely be uncontrollable. To entrust widows and orphans to them would be to put sheep into a tiger's jaws. “Nothing is impossible to a determined man. Fortunately, there's no hurry. Keep your eyes open and take your time.”

Suddenly, Yu looked excited and seemed about to speak. He had scarcely raised himself, however, before sinking back dejectedly. “No, no,” he muttered, shaking his head. Hu was puzzled. He could see nothing impracticable in his plan. “Why do you say no?” “I've thought of someone,” Yu said slowly. “But I'm afraid you wouldn't agree.” Now Hu understood. “You mean Shilong?” “Exactly. He's a great help to you. You couldn't let him go.” “That's true. But your affairs matter too. If Shilong himself really wished it, I could hardly object.” “We can discuss that another time.” Afraid of putting Hu in a difficult position, Yu drew back and changed the subject. “Tell me more about dividing my estate.”

“A daughter would ordinarily receive no share. But you've earned the property yourself, and nobody can tell you what to do with it. I suggest setting aside a sum for her first, in recognition of the bond between father and daughter.” Hu put this delicately. He meant that it would end A’lan's designs on her parents' property and prevent a great deal of trouble. Too deeply involved to see clearly, Yu had always supposed that his daughter acted from filial devotion. Only now did he begin to understand. Seeing the necessity, he nodded repeatedly. “I'll give her a hundred mu of farmland and twenty thousand taels in ready silver. And I shall speak plainly: she and her husband must show some conscience.” Hu could not readily respond to such words. After a pause, he went on. “Divide the rest into three shares. If A’hu's widow insists on remaining unmarried, she naturally deserves one. A’qi will have children in future, so she should have another. Keep the third in your own hands and decide what to do with it later. While you have that share, everyone will treat you dutifully. Whatever you do, don't give it all away! One more thing: once the division is settled, you must ask the authorities to put it on record, to prevent trouble later.”

“I understand. I'll do everything you say. Now...” Yu spoke with difficulty. “I'm only afraid A’qi still blames me.” “That's unavoidable.” Hu deliberately concealed A’qi's attachment to Chen and even told a lie. “She still remembers your kindness, really. For my sake, put up with a little humiliation. If she complains later, or even makes you look foolish, Brother Yu, you must bear with her.” “That's her temper. I won't take it to heart. From what you say, I'm to see her shortly. Where?” “We'll discuss that when Shilong comes back. For now, satisfy your craving, so that you'll have the energy to deal with A’qi later.” “Deal with” carried a double meaning. Yu gave an understanding smile, smoked his fill of opium as advised, and waited for good things to come in pairs. He had no idea what Hu had up his sleeve. Anxious and curious though he was, he must remain composed. With a faint smile, he dropped the subject of A’qi and asked about Hu's own affairs.

There was plenty to discuss. Hu had kept his dealings with You Laowu, particularly the inside story of the Small Swords Society, strictly secret even from Chen. With Yu, however, there was no need for concealment. They put their heads together and spoke so softly that only the two of them could hear. As Yu prepared the opium pellets, he listened intently. The account startled and thrilled him, and he regarded Hu with still greater respect. “I never imagined you'd been through all this!” he said when Hu finished. “It makes me wish I could go out and try my fortune in different places, as you have.” Seeing him encouraged, Hu seized the opportunity. “Brother Yu, these years are a time of great calamity, when the world is shaken to its foundations. I don't believe in saying that doom is inescapable. I think this is precisely the moment for a man to distinguish himself. If he spends his life fed and clothed, muddling through without a thought, he may look back as he closes his eyes and regret ever having come into the world. What would be the point of that?” “Exactly. A man leaves his name as a leopard leaves its skin. We must do one or two things others cannot do, so that, in life and after death, people will raise a thumb at the mention of our names and say, ‘That man had courage.’ Then we won't have disgraced our parents.” His tone reminded Hu of a saying he had heard from Ji Heling, and he repeated it at once. “‘An old steed in the stable still dreams of a thousand-mile journey.’ Brother Yu, if that's truly your ambition, there's an opportunity before you to accomplish something.”

“Oh? Tell me.” “They're organising a militia here in Huzhou. I hear Zhao Jingxian is a capable man. If you help him make a success of it, protecting the district and keeping the people safe, everyone will speak of you with admiration.” Yu said nothing. He blinked rapidly for some time, then suddenly put down his opium pipe and sat up. “You're right! Men or money, I'll provide all I can. But I can't very well go offering myself. It isn't that I want him to come begging for my advice. I'm afraid people would say I was reaching above my station, trying to push my way among the gentry and raise my own standing.” “That's hardly the way to look at it. Everyone has a duty to defend the district.” Hu paused briefly. “I'll arrange it. I'll ask Prefect Wang to speak to Zhao Jingxian. That will preserve your dignity as well.” “Good! You arrange it. I'll wait for your word.” He got down from the couch and told the bank's staff to prepare a meal. His spirits were excellent: the former dejection and listlessness had completely disappeared.

They had just raised their wine cups when Chen arrived. He nodded to Hu and sat down to eat with them. Yu knew that the arrangements were complete, but not what they were. When he saw A’qi, what should he say? He was burning to know, yet could hardly ask. The wine seemed to have lost its flavour. “Don't drink too much,” Hu said. “There'll be more later.” At that, Yu drained his cup and asked for rice. When he had finished eating, he sat to one side with his tea, waiting for Hu to act. “Let's go.” “Wait.” Yu could no longer keep silent. “Where?” “To the Dajing Silk Firm. I've asked A’qi to meet me there. You can hide in the back room and listen. Whatever is said, don't speak. Come out only when I call.” “And what am I to do then?” “Well...” Hu laughed. “That's between the two of you. How should I know?” The teasing words concealed their meaning: the broken mirror would be made whole, and the couple reunited. Naturally, Yu was excited and eager to leave.

The three left Jucheng Bank together but went separate ways. Yu accompanied Hu to Dajing; Chen had another destination. His first assignment had been to “lure the tiger away from the mountain.” He had hurried to Old Zhang and reported that Hu was in Huzhou and had important matters to discuss with Yu at Dajing, matters Huang Yi ought not to know about. Old Zhang and his wife were to invite Huang to their home on the pretext of discussing Chen's marriage, drink and talk with him, and make sure they kept him there. The purpose was to prevent an awkward meeting between Huang and A’qi when she came to Dajing. Now Chen knocked at A’qi's door. Her chief feeling was astonishment. Staring at him with her limpid eyes, she said only, “You!” “Yes, me,” Chen replied calmly. “One doesn't visit the temple without a reason.” “A reason? Hmph!” She gave a cold laugh. “You're a despicable creature. The dogs have eaten your conscience!” “Why start abusing me out of the blue?” “Why shouldn't I?” She thrust a finger against his forehead and pushed hard, her nail digging into his skin and leaving a red mark. “Keep your hands to yourself! Mr Hu has come from Hangzhou. He sent me to ask you over. He wants to talk to you.” “Still trying to deceive me! You really have no conscience left. Avoiding me yourself is one thing. But you sent Huang Yi to make a play for me, handing me over as a present to win his favour!” Growing angrier as she spoke, she shouted, “Get out! I don't want to see you.”

This reminded Chen of the scene that day, and he could not help laughing aloud. “You dare laugh? What's so funny?” “I'm laughing at a toad longing to eat swan's flesh. He very nearly had his eyes poked out.” “Oh!” Her eyes moved restlessly as she asked in puzzlement, “Did he really have the nerve to tell you about that glorious achievement?” “How could he tell me? I was watching from under the stairs next door. I saw it with my own eyes. Think about it, A’qi. Why would I play a trick on you? We're old acquaintances. Besides, you've entrusted your private savings to me to put out at interest. If I wronged you, wouldn't I be afraid of your pressing me for the money?” She looked a little embarrassed, then smiled. “Exactly! I'll make out that you owe me money. If you don't do as I say, I'll broadcast it all over town.” “Enough of that. Do you want to change your clothes? If not, let's go now.” “Mr Hu really wants to see me?” she asked instead of answering. “What does he want to say?” “I don't know. But I can tell you this: his luck is riding high. Anyone he looks after benefits. Take my advice and come.” He looked her over. Even in her everyday clothes, she had an unmistakable charm. “You look very pretty as you are. Don't bother changing.” She did as he said. After telling her sleepy young maid to keep an eye on the house, she went out with him. At the end of the lane they hired a small sedan chair, which carried her straight to Dajing.

“You grow younger every day!” Hu greeted her with a dose of flattery, then produced a foreign-made dressing mirror in chased silver, which he had specially asked Chen to borrow from A’zhu. “It's nothing very fine, Sister-in-Law Yu. A goose feather sent a thousand miles is a token of affection. I hope you'll find it useful.” “Thank you, Mr Hu. But I can't accept that form of address.” “Don't say that. Whatever quarrel you may have with Brother Yu, I shall always regard you as Sister-in-Law Yu.” “How could I aspire to a place in the Yu family? You do me a great honour, Mr Hu, and I'm very sorry, but you'll have to call me ungrateful for refusing it.” Finding her so guarded, Hu dared not rush matters. He invited her to sit and gave Chen a glance, signalling him to withdraw. “I'll be off, then,” Chen said. “See you tomorrow, A’qi.” “Wait.” Hu deliberately asked, “Where are you going? Is A’zhu waiting for you?” There was no need to think about the answer. Chen gave a firm, straightforward “Yes.” “Another man who'll be afraid of his wife!” Hu murmured as he watched Chen leave. A sidelong glance showed a look of emptiness and loss on A’qi's face. His little performance had worked. Once he had erased Chen's image from her heart, bringing her back to Yu would be easier.

“Mr Hu!” Composing herself, A’qi asked, “What did you wish to say to me? Please give me your instructions.” “I wouldn't presume to give instructions. Sister-in-Law Yu, the truth is that I came especially to see Brother Yu. At his age, to lose his only son—isn't it pitiful?” Resenting Yu, she wanted to answer that he deserved no pity. The words reached her lips, but she thought them too harsh and restrained herself, merely nodding. “I never met A’hu. What was he like?” “In all fairness, that young master of the Yu family was an exceptionally good man. Quite unlike his sister, who has her eyes on top of her forehead.” “Yes, I've heard you and the young lady don't get on. Is that true?” “You're only half right, Mr Hu. She's the one who doesn't get on with me!” A’qi said angrily. “Her father listened to his precious daughter and wanted to separate from me. Very well, then! I don't care about him either.” “Brother Yu has been a complete fool!” Hu took her side with an air of indignation. “You lowered yourself by going with him. How could he fail to appreciate his good fortune? I thought you had wanted to leave him. So he was the foolish one! I must give him a good talking-to.” A’qi fell into the trap and defended herself vigorously. “When did I ever want to leave him? The thought never entered my head. It was all his own doing. He still has his heart set on getting a couple of young ones. Old in years but young at heart—I don't know what ill-fated spell he's under!” “Excellent!” Hu raised his thumb. “Sister-in-Law Yu, I never realised how completely your heart belonged to him.” “Hmph! What good does that do?” She shook her head despondently. “There's no reward for being good. It makes one's heart turn cold.”

“There's no need for that. One must take a broader view...” “Exactly!” she interrupted. “That's what I think. There's no need to be narrow-minded. If the butcher dies, must we eat pigs with their bristles on? I'm not ashamed to say it: if I leave the Yu family, do you think I can't find another man? We'll see in the end which of us loses by it!” These disjointed words, full of jabs and thrusts, seemed broad-minded but really showed that she could not shake off Yu's hold on her. Hu felt he was doing well. Once he had discovered her true feelings, he was halfway to success. Taking up her words, he said, “Naturally, Brother Yu loses. Look at him now: lonely and miserable, lying awake all night thinking of his son. What sort of life is that?” She said nothing. After a pause, she observed, “He's brought it on himself.” “He has. But you've lost by it too.” “Well...” She shook her head emphatically. “I haven't lost anything.”

“How can you say that? How old are you now—twenty-something?” “I...” She hesitated, then answered honestly. “Twenty-seven.” “A woman is like a flower. At twenty-three or twenty-four, she's in full bloom. Once she reaches your age, she begins to age quickly. Think of it: you gave your best years to Brother Yu and have ended up with nothing. Isn't that a loss?” A’qi stared. She had never considered the matter in this light. Now that he pointed it out, the more she thought, the more reasonable it seemed—and the more wronged she felt. She could not help sighing. At this point, Hu fell silent. Taking a green-skinned, red-fleshed persimmon, he leisurely peeled it and waited for her feelings to break out. “Mr Hu, when I think of it, I've been treated terribly unfairly. Nobody is born degraded. To tell the truth, when I went with old Yu, I really meant to leave my trade and live respectably. Who could have imagined that, when you want to become a decent person, others refuse to let you?” As she spoke, a lifetime's grievances seemed to burst out together, and she became intensely agitated. “Just as you said, I gave him the best years of my life. Then he listened to his daughter and forced me to leave. If he can be so heartless, he mustn't blame me. I'll strip the respectability off his face.”

“Oh?” Hu asked calmly. “How will you do that?” “I'll...” She spoke with complete determination. “I'll go back to my old trade, and I'll still use his surname. I'll hang a sign with the name Yu at the door so that people can find me easily.” That was a formidable threat. If she carried it out, Yu's reputation would collapse. “A’qi, one mustn't drive things to a point of no return...” “He's forced me to it,” she interrupted. “You've only just thought of this, haven't you?” “Yes.” She was now completely under Hu's influence and said whatever came into her mind. “Thanks to your reminding me, Mr Hu, I can see what an intolerable wrong I've suffered.” “Then I've become the one stirring up trouble. A’qi, spare a thought for me.” “I'm sorry!” Her face was full of contrition. “But I have to do it. Please understand.” “All you want is to vent your anger. What if I find another way for you?” She thought, then answered, “Tell me what you have in mind.” She immediately added, “That doesn't mean I've changed my mind. Whether you speak is up to you; whether I agree is up to me.”

“Of course. It's not only you who feels this wrong must be put right. Even as an outsider, I can't accept it. Whatever happens, you must regain your dignity and vindicate yourself. Regaining your dignity is a vindication, isn't it?” A’qi did not think his words quite right, but could not see what was wrong with them either. She answered vaguely, “Tell me your plan first.” “I mean to make Brother Yu apologise to you. How would that be?” “Apologise?” she asked blankly. “How?” “How would you like him to? Surely you don't want a formal settlement over tea?” Such a tea meeting was a custom among people of the streets and waterways: any grievance was openly stated and settled face to face. There was no precedent for using it in a domestic dispute like this. Yet A’qi could think of no other way to make Yu apologise. She merely stared at Hu, her wide eyes showing more black than white. “A’qi, apologies and all the rest are empty forms. A person's feelings are what count. If Brother Yu gives you his true heart, surely that should be enough.” On the one hand, she felt there was something in this; on the other, she suspected a deeper meaning. The two thoughts together required careful consideration. Resting her hands on her knees, she lowered her head and eyes. Only her lashes kept moving. Her quiet, composed posture was strikingly attractive.

She was still considering his words, but Hu felt that he had gone too far round the subject and was growing impatient himself. He decided to reveal the answer. After a moment's thought, he said, “Sister-in-Law Yu, you've already had some satisfaction. You've called him heartless one moment and an old fool the next, scolding him mercilessly, and he hasn't answered a word. That's as good as an apology. You can afford to let your anger cool.” A’qi was bewildered. Only after a long pause did she say, “I've been like someone calling the emperor a fool behind his back. He isn't here. How could he hear?” “Who says he isn't here?” Hu tapped the partition. “Brother Yu, you can come out now and say a few kind words to Sister-in-Law Yu.” “Yes!” Yu answered, lifting the curtain. Slightly embarrassed, he began, “A’qi!” Only now did she understand. At the sight of her troublesome lover, her first feeling was anger. She turned to leave, only to find an ambush at the door. Chen's claim that he was going to the Zhangs had been false; he had been waiting outside all along. Smiling, he said, “You mustn't leave! If you do, you'll miss Fourth Uncle kneeling on an abacus and balancing an oil lamp on his head.” This provoked her again. “A fine fellow you are!” she said, glaring. “You've joined him in playing tricks on me!” “Yes, yes!” Clasping his hands high, Chen bowed to the ground. “I was wrong. Don't be angry.” Now she was at a loss. Neither force nor persuasion would serve. She could not get away, yet she refused to acknowledge Yu. All she could do was turn back and sit down, facing the window, her expression rigid and her lips closed.

“A’qi!” Yu began. “Let's say I was wrong...” “You were wrong!” She turned sharply and cut him short. “Yes, yes!” Like Chen, Yu yielded on every point. “I was wrong. It was all my fault. There, it's over now. We needn't trouble Mr Hu any longer. Let's go.” “Go? Where?” “You tell me. My place or yours?” “Your place? Hmph!” She gave a cold laugh. “The Yu family has a lofty threshold. How could I ever step over it?” Once she had reached this sort of sour remark, all that remained was a matter of time and patience. Hu gave Chen a glance and rose. “Good! There's no need for us to stay here making nuisances of ourselves. Have a few words together. Later, I'll escort you to the bridal chamber.” “What bridal chamber?” A’qi stood to stop him. “Don't go, Mr Hu. We must get things straight. It isn't as easy as that!” “I'm not leaving. I'll be in the room opposite. Talk it over yourselves first. If you agree, all the better. If you don't, call and I'll come. Don't worry, Sister-in-Law Yu. I'm on your side.”

This promise was another invisible cord binding her more tightly. Apart from continuing to call Yu heartless and an old fool, she put forward only one condition: he must never let his daughter enter his house again. How could he possibly do that? However gently he reasoned with her, she would not give way. They had to call Hu back to mediate. After hearing the difficulty, Hu smiled at Yu. “She's deliberately making things hard for you. Sister-in-Law Yu is a reasonable woman.” This was the device known as the Golden Bell Shield: one sentence enclosed her completely. Having been praised for being reasonable, she could hardly declare herself unreasonable and insist that Yu sever all contact with his daughter. So once again she sat with a stiff face and said nothing. “Now I understand,” Hu told Yu. “Sister-in-Law isn't angry with you. She's angry with your daughter. And no wonder! I'd be angry too. When you consider it, she has been treated very unfairly. Naturally, she wants you to put matters right. But, after all, you're one family. Could she really force you to disown your daughter? Even if you agreed, she wouldn't want people calling her an unworthy woman. As they say in Shandong, a piece of tofu has fallen into a heap of ash: you can't flick it clean. She truly has a grievance she can't express.” These words went straight to the feelings in A’qi's heart. She had sensed them herself but had been unable to put them into words. Now Hu had spoken for her. The relief thrilled her, mingling with gratitude that there was, after all, someone in the world who understood her. It was like a cup of hot vinegar poured over her heart. She began to sob.

She wept and reproached Yu as she wept, but this was no longer a quarrel: it was a pouring out of grievances. Although somewhat embarrassed, Yu felt a weight lift from his heart. He knew the great matter was settled. With his mind at ease, he could respond calmly. Saying nothing, he drew a handkerchief from his sleeve and passed it to her to dry her eyes. By the time she had soaked it and stopped crying, gratitude far outweighed resentment in her heart. Her gratitude was towards Hu. Rising, she made him a curtsy. “Mr Hu, thank you! I've taken up so much of your time and energy.” Then she turned to Yu. “It's time to go. We've troubled Mr Hu for ages, and still you sit here!” “Yes, yes, let's go!” Yu answered eagerly. “But first tell me where.” “Where else? Home, of course.” “Yes, yes! Home!” He turned to Hu, seemingly with a thousand things to say and unable to begin. At last he managed, “We'll talk again tomorrow.” A thunderstorm had turned into a spring breeze. Hu felt wonderfully at ease as, smiling faintly, he saw them out. In the front shop they came face to face with Huang Yi. Both he and Hu were surprised and stopped involuntarily. “Mr Huang!” A’qi greeted him with perfect composure, lifting a hand. “See you tomorrow.” With a smile back over her shoulder, she went away in triumph.
